title: Electrostatic Potential & Capacitance
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Electrostatic Potential Energy, Potential of Continuous Bodies (Ring, Disk, Shells, Solid Sphere), E = -grad V, Dipole Potential, Conductors & Earthing, Capacitors, Dielectrics & Charge Sharing
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: Why Use Scalar Potential Instead of Vector Field?

In Chapter 15, calculating the net Electric Field $\vec{E}$ required resolving 3D vectors into $x, y, z$ components at every step. Just as we introduced scalar Potential Energy ($U$) in Mechanics to bypass complicated vector force equations, we now introduce Electrostatic Potential ($V$) in Electrodynamics.

What Is Electric Potential ($V$)?
Because the electrostatic force is strictly conservative ($\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} = 0$), the work done in moving a test charge $q_0$ from infinity ($\infty$) to any point $P$ is independent of the path taken. Electric Potential ($V$) at point $P$ is the electrostatic potential energy per unit charge at that point: $$\boxed{V_P = \frac{U_P}{q_0} = \frac{W_{\text{ext}}(\infty \to P)}{q_0} = -\int_{\infty}^{P} \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}} \qquad \left(\text{SI Unit: } 1\text{ Volt (V)} = 1\text{ J/C}\right)$$Because $V$ is a pure scalar, finding the net potential of 100 charges is simple algebraic addition (including $+$ or $-$ signs of the charges)!

topics.title: Electrostatic Potential & Potential Energy, Work Done, Continuous Charge Potentials (Ring, Disk, Spheres) & E = -grad V
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Potential Difference, Work Done & Potential Energy of a System of Point Charges
$$\text{Potential Difference } (V_B - V_A): \qquad \boxed{V_B - V_A = \frac{U_B - U_A}{q} = \frac{W_{\text{ext, slow}}(A \to B)}{q} = -\frac{W_{\text{electric field}}(A \to B)}{q} = -\int_A^B \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}}$$
  • Work Done by External Agent (Slowly, $\Delta K = 0$): $\boxed{W_{\text{ext}} = +q(V_{\text{final}} - V_{\text{initial}})}$.
  • Work Done by the Electric Field Itself: $\boxed{W_{\text{field}} = -\Delta U = +q(V_{\text{initial}} - V_{\text{final}})}$.
  • Interaction Potential Energy of Point Charges:
    • For 2 charges $q_1, q_2$ at distance $r$: $\boxed{U = \frac{k q_1 q_2}{r}}$ (Substitute charges WITH their $+$ or $-$ signs!).
    • For 3 charges ($3$ pairs): $U = k\left(\frac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}} + \frac{q_2 q_3}{r_{23}} + \frac{q_3 q_1}{r_{31}}\right)$.
    • For $N$ charges: Total number of unique pairs is $\binom{N}{2} = \frac{N(N-1)}{2}$, and $U = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N q_i V_i$.
1.2 Master Electric Potential Dictionary for Continuous Bodies (Reference $V(\infty) = 0$)
Charged BodyPoint LocationElectric Potential Formula $V$
1. Point Charge $Q$At distance $r$$$\boxed{V(r) = \frac{kQ}{r} = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}}$$
2. Uniformly Charged Ring
(Charge $Q$, radius $R$)		On axis at distance $x$ from center$$\boxed{V(x) = \frac{kQ}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}} \qquad \left(\text{At center } x = 0: \; V_0 = \frac{kQ}{R}\right)$$
3. Uniformly Charged Disk
(Surface density $\sigma$, radius $R$)		On axis at distance $x$ from center$$\boxed{V(x) = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{R^2 + x^2} - x\right)}$$
4. Hollow Spherical Shell / Conducting Sphere
(Charge $Q$, radius $R$)		Inside ($r \le R$) vs. Outside ($r > R$)$$\boxed{V_{\text{in}} = \frac{kQ}{R} = V_{\text{surface}} = \text{Constant!}}, \qquad \boxed{V_{\text{out}} = \frac{kQ}{r}}$$
5. Uniform Solid Non-Conducting Sphere
(Charge $Q$, radius $R$)		Inside ($r \le R$) vs. Outside ($r > R$)$$\boxed{V_{\text{in}}(r) = \frac{kQ}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)}, \qquad \boxed{V_{\text{out}}(r) = \frac{kQ}{r}}$$
($\text{At center } r = 0: \; \boxed{V_{\text{center}} = \frac{3}{2}\frac{kQ}{R} = 1.5\,V_{\text{surface}}}$!)
1.3 Finding Electric Field $\vec{E}$ from Potential $V(x, y, z)$ (Potential Gradient)
$$\boxed{\vec{E} = -\nabla V = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{For Radial Symmetry:} \quad \boxed{E_r = -\frac{dV}{dr}}$$

Physical Rule: The Electric Field vector $\vec{E}$ ALWAYS points in the direction of steepest DECREASE of electric potential $V$, and is always perpendicular to Equipotential Surfaces!
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Potential Inside a Uniform Solid Non-Conducting Sphere: V_in = (kQ / 2R³)(3R² − r²)

At any point $r < R$ inside a solid non-conducting sphere, the electric field is $E_{\text{in}}(r) = \frac{kQr}{R^3}$, and at the surface ($r = R$) the potential is $V(R) = \frac{kQ}{R}$. Using $V(r) - V(R) = -\int_R^r E_{\text{in}}\,dr$:

$$V(r) - \frac{kQ}{R} = -\int_R^r \frac{kQr}{R^3}\,dr = -\frac{kQ}{R^3}\left[\frac{r^2 - R^2}{2}\right] = \frac{kQ}{2R^3}(R^2 - r^2)$$

Adding $\frac{kQ}{R} = \frac{2kQ R^2}{2R^3}$ to both sides gives the famous parabolic potential formula:

$$\boxed{V_{\text{in}}(r) = \frac{kQ}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)} \qquad \left(\text{At } r = 0: \; V_{\text{center}} = \frac{3kQ}{2R} = \frac{3}{2}V_{\text{surface}}\right)$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Inside a Hollow Shell, $E = 0$ Does NOT Mean $V = 0$!): Because $E_{\text{in}} = -\frac{dV}{dr} = 0$, the potential $V$ inside a hollow conducting or non-conducting shell is CONSTANT (and equal to the surface potential $\frac{kQ}{R}$), NOT zero!
  • Trap 2 (Non-Uniformly Charged Ring Still Has $V = \frac{kQ}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}$ on Its Axis!): Even if charge $Q$ is distributed completely non-uniformly around a ring of radius $R$, every charge element $dq$ is at the exact same distance $\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}$ from any axial point, so the axial potential is STILL $\frac{kQ}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}$! (However, the electric field is no longer purely axial if the ring is non-uniform).

topics.title: Potential of an Electric Dipole, Equipotential Surfaces, Properties of Conductors, Concentric Shells, Earthing & Self-Energy
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Electrostatic Potential of a Short Electric Dipole ($r \gg a$)
$$\boxed{V(r, \theta) = \frac{k (\vec{p}\cdot\vec{r})}{r^3} = \frac{k p \cos\theta}{r^2} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}}$$
  • On the Axial Line ($\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$): $V_{\text{axial}} = \pm\frac{kp}{r^2}$ ($+$ near $+q$, $-$ near $-q$), while $E_{\text{axial}} = \frac{2kp}{r^3} \neq 0$.
  • On the Entire Equatorial Plane ($\theta = 90^\circ$): $\cos 90^\circ = 0 \implies \boxed{V_{\text{equatorial}} = 0}$ everywhere on the equatorial plane, even though $\vec{E}_{\text{eq}} = -\frac{k\vec{p}}{r^3} \neq 0$! Therefore, zero work is needed to move any test charge anywhere along the equatorial plane of a dipole.
2.2 Conductors in Electrostatic Equilibrium, Concentric Shells & Earthing (Grounding)
The 5 Golden Laws of Conductors in Electrostatic Equilibrium:
  1. Zero Internal Field: $\vec{E}_{\text{inside metal}} = 0$ everywhere inside the bulk material of the conductor.
  2. Equipotential Volume: The entire conductor (interior + surface) is at a single constant potential $V$.
  3. Surface Charge Only: Any net excess charge resides strictly on the outer surface ($q_{\text{interior}} = 0$), with local density $\sigma \propto \frac{1}{R_{\text{curvature}}}$ (highest at sharp points — Corona Discharge).
  4. Perpendicular Surface Field: Just outside the surface, $\vec{E} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}$ is strictly perpendicular to the surface.
  5. Electrostatic Shielding (Faraday Cage): An empty cavity inside a closed conductor is 100% shielded from any external electric fields ($\vec{E}_{\text{cavity}} = 0$).

Concentric Conducting Spherical Shells (Radii $R_1 < R_2$, Charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$):
By superposition, the potential of a shell of radius $r$ due to its own charge is $\frac{kQ}{r}$, due to an inner shell is $\frac{kQ_{\text{in}}}{r}$ (since it lies outside the inner shell), and due to an outer shell of radius $R_{\text{out}}$ is $\frac{kQ_{\text{out}}}{R_{\text{out}}}$ (since it lies inside the outer shell!):

$$\text{Potential of Inner Shell } (R_1): \quad \boxed{V_1 = k\left(\frac{Q_1}{R_1} + \frac{Q_2}{R_2}\right)} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Potential of Outer Shell } (R_2): \quad \boxed{V_2 = k\left(\frac{Q_1 + Q_2}{R_2}\right)}$$

What Happens When a Shell Is Earthed (Grounded)?
Earthing connects the conductor to the Earth, forcing its NET POTENTIAL to be ZERO ($V_{\text{earthed}} = 0$) (NOT its charge to be zero!):
• If Outer Shell ($R_2$) is earthed ($V_2 = 0$): $Q_1 + Q_2' = 0 \implies \boxed{Q_2' = -Q_1}$ (total charge on outer shell becomes $-Q_1$).
• If Inner Shell ($R_1$) is earthed ($V_1 = 0$): $\frac{Q_1'}{R_1} + \frac{Q_2}{R_2} = 0 \implies \boxed{Q_1' = -\left(\frac{R_1}{R_2}\right)Q_2}$!

$$\textbf{Electrostatic Self-Energy of Spheres:} \qquad \boxed{U_{\text{hollow shell}} = \frac{kQ^2}{2R} = \frac{Q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 R}}, \qquad \boxed{U_{\text{solid non-conducting}} = \frac{3}{5}\frac{kQ^2}{R}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Why Connecting an Inner Shell (R₁) to an Outer Surrounding Shell (R₂) Transfers 100% of Q₁ to the Outer Shell!

From the concentric shell equations above, subtract $V_2$ from $V_1$ to find the potential difference between the inner and outer shells:

$$\boxed{V_1 - V_2 = k Q_1 \left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)}$$

Look closely at this remarkable result: The potential difference $V_1 - V_2$ depends ONLY on the inner charge $Q_1$ and is completely independent of the outer charge $Q_2$! Therefore, if you connect the inner shell to the outer shell with a conducting wire ($V_1 = V_2$), we must have $Q_1 = 0$—meaning $100\%$ of the inner shell's charge flows to the outer shell, no matter how much charge the outer shell already has! (This is the principle of the Van de Graaff Generator).

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Charge Distribution on Parallel Conducting Plates $Q_1, Q_2$): When two large parallel conducting plates are given charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, the outermost faces (leftmost of plate 1 and rightmost of plate 2) ALWAYS carry the average charge $\boxed{q_{\text{outer}} = \frac{Q_1 + Q_2}{2}}$, while the two facing inner surfaces carry equal and opposite charges $\boxed{q_{\text{inner}} = \pm\left(\frac{Q_1 - Q_2}{2}\right)}$!

topics.title: Capacitance: Parallel-Plate, Spherical & Cylindrical Capacitors, Series/Parallel Networks, Stored Energy & Heat Loss
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Capacitance ($C = Q/V$) of Standard Geometries
Definition of Capacitance ($C$):
For any two-conductor system carrying charges $+Q$ and $-Q$ with potential difference $V$, the ratio $C = \frac{Q}{V}$ is a constant that depends ONLY on the geometry (size, shape, separation) and the dielectric medium—never on $Q$ or $V$! (SI Unit: $1\text{ Farad (F)} = 1\text{ C/V}$).
Capacitor GeometryCapacitance Formula (in Vacuum, multiply by $K$ for dielectric)
1. Isolated Conducting Sphere (Radius $R$, outer shell at $\infty$)$$\boxed{C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R = \frac{R}{k}} \qquad (\text{For Earth } R = 6400\text{ km}: \; C \approx 711\,\mu\text{F})$$
2. Parallel-Plate Capacitor (Plate area $A$, separation $d \ll \sqrt{A}$)$$\boxed{C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}} \qquad \left(\text{Uniform Field } E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A} = \frac{V}{d}\right)$$
3. Spherical Capacitor (Concentric shells $a < b$, outer shell earthed)$$\boxed{C = \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a b}{b - a}} \qquad \left(\text{If INNER shell } a \text{ is earthed, } V \text{ on outer } b: \; \boxed{C = \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 b^2}{b - a}}\right)$$
4. Cylindrical Capacitor (Coaxial cylinders $a < b$, length $L \gg b$)$$\boxed{C = \frac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)}}$$
3.2 Series & Parallel Combinations, Stored Energy, Force Between Plates & Charge Sharing
CombinationSame QuantityEquivalent Capacitance ($C_{\text{eq}}$)Voltage / Charge Division Rule
1. Series CombinationSame Charge $Q$$$\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} \implies C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}$$$V \propto \frac{1}{C} \implies V_1 = \left(\frac{C_2}{C_1 + C_2}\right)V$
2. Parallel CombinationSame Voltage $V$$$C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2$$$Q \propto C \implies Q_1 = \left(\frac{C_1}{C_1 + C_2}\right)Q_{\text{total}}$
$$\textbf{Energy Stored in Capacitor:} \quad \boxed{U = \frac{1}{2}C V^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}Q V} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \textbf{Electric Field Energy Density:} \quad \boxed{u_E = \frac{U}{A d} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2}$$
$$\textbf{Attractive Force Between Parallel Capacitor Plates:} \qquad \boxed{F = \frac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0 A} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 A E^2} \qquad \left(\text{Electrostatic Pressure } P_e = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\right)$$

Connecting Two Charged Capacitors ($C_1, V_1$ and $C_2, V_2$) in Parallel:

$$\text{Common Potential:} \quad \boxed{V_c = \frac{Q_{\text{net}}}{C_1 + C_2} = \frac{C_1 V_1 \pm C_2 V_2}{C_1 + C_2}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Heat Loss:} \quad \boxed{\Delta H = U_i - U_f = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}\right)(V_1 \mp V_2)^2}$$

Sign Note: Use $+V_2$ in $V_c$ (and $-V_2$ in $\Delta H$) when positive plate is connected to positive plate; use $-V_2$ in $V_c$ (and $+V_2$ in $\Delta H$) when positive plate is connected to negative plate (reverse polarity)!
topics.derivationHtml:
Why the Force Between Capacitor Plates Has a Factor of 1/2 (F = Q² / 2ε₀A) & Why Charging Wastes 50% Energy as Heat

1. Plate Attraction Force: Why is the force on plate 2 ($+Q$) equal to $F = Q\left(\frac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0 A}\right) = \frac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0 A}$ instead of $Q E_{\text{total}} = Q\left(\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A}\right)$? Because a plate cannot exert a force on itself! The field $\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ between the plates is the sum of $\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ from plate 1 and $\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ from plate 2. Plate 2 sits only in the field of plate 1 ($E_1 = \frac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0 A}$), so $F = Q E_1 = \boxed{\frac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0 A}}$!

2. Battery Work vs. Stored Energy: When an uncharged capacitor $C$ is connected to a battery of EMF $V$, the battery pumps charge $Q = CV$ through constant potential difference $V$, doing work $\boxed{W_{\text{battery}} = Q V = C V^2}$. Since the capacitor stores only $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$, the remaining $\boxed{H = W_{\text{battery}} - \Delta U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2}$ (exactly $50\%$) is dissipated as heat in the connecting wires!

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Flipping Battery Polarity on an Already Charged Capacitor $C$): If a capacitor charged to $+Q = +CV$ has its battery connections reversed (so final charge is $-Q = -CV$), the charge moved through the battery is $\Delta q = Q_f - Q_i = \mathbf{2CV}$! Thus work done by the battery is $W_{\text{batt}} = (2CV)V = 2CV^2$, while $\Delta U = U_f - U_i = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 - \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = 0$, so total heat dissipated is $\boxed{H = 2CV^2}$ (NOT $\frac{1}{2}CV^2$)!

topics.title: Dielectrics in Capacitors: Induced Bound Charge, Battery Connected vs. Disconnected & Composite Dielectric Slabs
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Dielectric Polarization, Induced Charge ($q_i$) & Partial Slab Formula
How a Dielectric Slab ($K$) Increases Capacitance ($C = K C_0$):
When an insulating dielectric of constant $K$ is placed between capacitor plates carrying free charge $\pm Q$, its molecules polarize, creating bound induced surface charges $\mp q_i$ that oppose the external field $E_0$ and reduce the net field inside the dielectric to $E = \frac{E_0}{K}$!
$$\textbf{Induced Bound Charge:} \qquad \boxed{q_i = Q\left(1 - \frac{1}{K}\right)} \qquad \left(\text{For a metal slab } K = \infty: \; q_i = Q\right)$$

Partially Filled Capacitor (Slab of Thickness $t < d$ and Dielectric Constant $K$):
The air gap has thickness $(d - t)$ with field $E_0 = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$, and the slab has thickness $t$ with field $\frac{E_0}{K}$. Thus $V = E_0(d - t) + \frac{E_0}{K}t = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A}\left(d - t + \frac{t}{K}\right)$:

$$\boxed{C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t + \frac{t}{K}}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{For multiple slabs } (t_1, t_2, \dots): \quad \boxed{C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - (t_1 + t_2 + \dots) + \frac{t_1}{K_1} + \frac{t_2}{K_2} + \dots}}$$

Special Case (Conducting Metal Slab of Thickness $t$, $K = \infty$): $\boxed{C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t}}$. (However, inserting an infinitely thin foil $t \to 0$ does not change $C$ unless the foil is connected to one of the plates!)

4.2 Master Comparison Table: Inserting a Dielectric ($K$) with Battery Disconnected vs. Connected
Physical QuantityCase A: Battery DISCONNECTED (Isolated, $Q = Q_0 = \text{Constant}$)Case B: Battery Remains CONNECTED ($V = V_0 = \text{Constant}$)
1. Capacitance ($C$)Increases $K$ times: $C = K C_0$Increases $K$ times: $C = K C_0$
2. Charge on Plates ($Q$)Remains Constant: $Q = Q_0$Increases $K$ times: $Q = K Q_0$
3. Potential Difference ($V$)Decreases $K$ times: $V = \frac{V_0}{K}$Remains Constant: $V = V_0$
4. Electric Field ($E = V/d$)Decreases $K$ times: $E = \frac{E_0}{K}$Remains Constant: $E = E_0$
5. Stored Energy ($U$)Decreases $K$ times: $U = \frac{Q_0^2}{2(KC_0)} = \frac{U_0}{K}$Increases $K$ times: $U = \frac{1}{2}(KC_0)V_0^2 = K U_0$
4.3 Distance-Split (Series) vs. Area-Split (Parallel) Dielectrics ($K_1$ and $K_2$)
  • 1. Distance Split (Half thickness $d/2$ has $K_1$, other half $d/2$ has $K_2$): The two halves are in SERIES:
    $$\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} \implies \boxed{K_{\text{eq, series}} = \frac{2 K_1 K_2}{K_1 + K_2} = \text{Harmonic Mean}}$$
  • 2. Area Split (Half area $A/2$ has $K_1$, other half $A/2$ has $K_2$ across full gap $d$): The two halves are in PARALLEL:
    $$C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 \implies \boxed{K_{\text{eq, parallel}} = \frac{K_1 + K_2}{2} = \text{Arithmetic Mean}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Why a Capacitor Sucks In a Dielectric Slab: Attractive Fringe-Field Force F = ½ (K − 1)(ε₀ b d / d²) V²

Suppose a dielectric slab of width $b$, length $L$, and thickness $d$ is inserted a distance $x$ into a capacitor of plate size $L \times b$ connected to a battery of constant voltage $V$. At insertion depth $x$, the capacitance is the parallel sum of the filled part ($x$) and the air part ($L - x$):

$$C(x) = \frac{K\varepsilon_0 b x}{d} + \frac{\varepsilon_0 b(L - x)}{d} = \frac{\varepsilon_0 b}{d}\left[L + (K - 1)x\right]$$

At constant voltage $V$, the electrostatic force pulling the dielectric slab inward is:

$$\boxed{F_{\text{inward}} = \frac{1}{2}V^2 \frac{dC}{dx} = \frac{\varepsilon_0 b (K - 1)V^2}{2d}} \qquad (\text{Constant inward force, independent of } x!)$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Dielectric Breakdown Voltage of Series Capacitors): When two capacitors $C_1$ (breakdown voltage $V_{1,\max}$) and $C_2$ (breakdown voltage $V_{2,\max}$) are connected in series, they must carry the SAME charge $Q$. Therefore, the maximum safe charge the series combination can hold without either capacitor sparking is $\boxed{Q_{\max} = \min(C_1 V_{1,\max}, \; C_2 V_{2,\max})}$, and the maximum safe total voltage is $\boxed{V_{\text{total, max}} = \frac{Q_{\max}}{C_{\text{eq}}}}$ (NEVER $V_{1,\max} + V_{2,\max}$)!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 16: Electrostatic Potential & Capacitance! Next, in Chapter 17, we let charges flow continuously through conductors to master Current Electricity and RC Circuits.
summary:
• Potential & Field: $V = \frac{kQ}{r}$, $\vec{E} = -\nabla V$; Solid sphere center $V_{\text{center}} = 1.5\,V_{\text{surface}}$; Shell $V_{\text{in}} = V_{\text{surface}} = \frac{kQ}{R}$.
  • Dipole Potential: $V = \frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}$ ($0$ on equatorial plane).
  • Capacitance: Parallel plate $C = \frac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$; Spherical $C = \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 ab}{b-a}$; Stored energy $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$.
  • Charge Sharing: $V_c = \frac{C_1 V_1 \pm C_2 V_2}{C_1 + C_2}$ and $\Delta H = \frac{1}{2}\frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}(V_1 \mp V_2)^2$.
  • Dielectrics: Induced charge $q_i = Q\left(1 - \frac{1}{K}\right)$; Partial slab $C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t + t/K}$.

questions.prompt: In a region of space, the electrostatic potential is given by $V(x, y, z) = (4x^2 - 3y + 2z)\text{ Volts}$, where $x, y, z$ are in metres. What is the electric field vector $\vec{E}$ at the point $(1\text{ m}, 2\text{ m}, 3\text{ m})$?
questions.explanation: Using $\vec{E} = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right) = -(8x\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$. Substituting $x = 1\text{ m}$ gives $\vec{E} = (-8\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k})\text{ V/m}$.

questions.prompt: 27 identical small spherical mercury drops, each charged to a potential of $V_0 = 10\text{ V}$, coalesce to form a single large spherical drop. What is the electrostatic potential of the large drop?
questions.explanation: When $N$ identical drops of radius $r$ and charge $q$ merge: total charge $Q = Nq$ and new radius $R = N^{1/3}r$. Therefore, $V_{\text{big}} = \frac{kQ}{R} = \frac{k(Nq)}{N^{1/3}r} = N^{2/3}V_0$. For $N = 27$: $V_{\text{big}} = (27)^{2/3}(10\text{ V}) = 9 \times 10 = 90\text{ V}$.

questions.prompt: A capacitor of capacitance $C_1 = 4\,\mu\text{F}$ is charged to a potential of $V_1 = 100\text{ V}$. The battery is then disconnected and this capacitor is connected in parallel to an uncharged capacitor of capacitance $C_2 = 2\,\mu\text{F}$. What is the common potential $V_c$ and the energy lost as heat during charge redistribution?
questions.explanation: Common potential $V_c = \frac{C_1 V_1 + 0}{C_1 + C_2} = \frac{4(100)}{4 + 2} = \frac{400}{6} = 66.7\text{ V}$. Heat loss $\Delta H = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}\right)(V_1 - 0)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4 \times 2}{4 + 2}\times 10^{-6}\right)(100)^2 = \frac{4}{6}\times 10^{-2}\text{ J} = 6.67\text{ mJ}$.

questions.prompt: Two capacitors $C_1 = 2\,\mu\text{F}$ (maximum breakdown voltage $6\text{ kV}$) and $C_2 = 4\,\mu\text{F}$ (maximum breakdown voltage $4\text{ kV}$) are connected in series across a high-voltage DC source. What is the maximum total voltage that can be safely applied across the series combination without puncturing either capacitor?
questions.explanation: Maximum safe charges are $Q_{1,\max} = C_1 V_{1,\max} = 2 \times 6 = 12\text{ mC}$ and $Q_{2,\max} = C_2 V_{2,\max} = 4 \times 4 = 16\text{ mC}$. In series, both capacitors carry the same charge, so $Q_{\max} = \min(12, 16) = 12\text{ mC}$. Since $C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{2 \times 4}{2 + 4} = \frac{4}{3}\,\mu\text{F}$, maximum safe voltage is $V_{\max} = \frac{Q_{\max}}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{12}{4/3} = 9\text{ kV}$.

questions.prompt: A parallel-plate air capacitor has capacitance $C_0$. Half of the space between the plates (thickness $d/2$, full area $A$) is filled with a dielectric of constant $K_1 = 3$, and the remaining half thickness $d/2$ is filled with a dielectric of constant $K_2 = 6$. What is the new capacitance of the capacitor?
questions.explanation: For a distance split ($d/2$ and $d/2$), the two dielectric layers are in series, so $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{2 K_1 K_2}{K_1 + K_2} = \frac{2(3)(6)}{3 + 6} = \frac{36}{9} = 4$. Thus $C = 4\,C_0$.

questions.prompt: A solid non-conducting sphere of radius $R$ carries a uniform volume charge distribution. If the electrostatic potential at the surface of the sphere is $V_{\text{surface}} = 20\text{ V}$ (taking $V(\infty) = 0$), what is the potential at the center of the sphere?
questions.explanation: For a uniformly charged solid non-conducting sphere, $V_{\text{center}} = \frac{3}{2}V_{\text{surface}} = 1.5 \times 20\text{ V} = 30\text{ V}$.

questions.prompt: Two concentric conducting spherical shells have radii $R_1 = a$ and $R_2 = 2a$. The outer shell is given a charge $+Q$, while the inner shell is connected to the Earth (grounded, $V_1 = 0$). What is the charge $q_1$ induced on the inner shell?
questions.explanation: Potential of the inner shell of radius $a$ is $V_1 = k\left(\frac{q_1}{a} + \frac{Q}{2a}\right) = 0 \implies q_1 = -\frac{a}{2a}Q = -\frac{Q}{2}$.

questions.prompt: An air capacitor of capacitance $C_0 = 2\,\mu\text{F}$ is connected to a $V_0 = 100\text{ V}$ battery. While the battery remains connected, a dielectric slab of constant $K = 3$ is slowly inserted to completely fill the space between the plates. How much extra work is done by the battery during the insertion of the slab?
questions.explanation: Initial charge $Q_i = C_0 V_0 = 200\,\mu\text{C}$. Final charge $Q_f = K C_0 V_0 = 3(200) = 600\,\mu\text{C}$. Extra charge supplied by the battery is $\Delta q = Q_f - Q_i = 400\,\mu\text{C}$. Therefore, work done by the battery is $W_{\text{battery}} = (\Delta q)V_0 = (400 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C})(100\text{ V}) = 0.04\text{ J} = 40\text{ mJ}$ (of which $20\text{ mJ}$ increases stored energy $\Delta U$, and $20\text{ mJ}$ goes into mechanical work/heat).
